paper_title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions, supporting policy evaluation and model-based planning (Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). Accurate simulation requires modeling robot motion and resulting scene changes. Latent action models encode visual transitions as proxy actions (Bruce et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025), allowing world models to learn dynamics from large-scale videos without explicit action annotations (Gao et al., 2026). These latent actions are learned through future-observation reconstruction, with the current observation providing visual context (Gao et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026). For action-conditioned simulation, inferred latent actions serve as supervision for mapping robot controls into the learned latent action space. Learning this mapping is challenging since reconstruction objectives encourage latent actions to encode robot motion together with object responses and other scene changes (Nikulin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). For example, similar end-effector motions may produce different object responses under different contact states (Gu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), introducing scene-dependent variation beyond robot motion into the adaptation target. These interaction outcomes are useful for world modeling, since accurate simulation requires predicting how robot motion affects the surrounding scene. This motivates dedicated kinematic component for action adaptation, together with residual component retaining complementary transition information for dynamics learning. To this end, we propose SkeLAM, skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. Robot skeletons describe robot configuration and motion while abstracting scene appearance. Related robot world models use skeleton sequences or kinematic renderings as direct conditioning signals for generation (Wang et al., 2025b; Wu & Gao, 2026; Xu et al., 2026). SkeLAM uses paired RGB and skeleton transitions to learn kinematic and residual components from RGB 1 Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models observations. Skeleton supervision grounds the kinematic latent in robot motion, while the residual latent supplies complementary information for RGB reconstruction. Together, the two components jointly support reconstruction, providing dedicated target for action adaptation while retaining information for dynamics learning. During representation learning, skeletons supervise the RGB latents, while the deployed interface uses RGB observations and robot actions. We further introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction, which replaces the RGB kinematic latent with its paired skeleton counterpart while retaining the RGB residual. Reconstructing the same transition under this substitution encourages compatible motion conditioning in the RGB decoder, extending cross-modal correspondence beyond alignment in latent space. The world model learns from both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout prepares it for the zero-residual condition used at deployment. lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, generation uses the current observation and robot actions. To assess motion accuracy and visual fidelity, we evaluate SkeLAM on DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024). Compared with DreamDojo, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1%. Motion probing shows that the kinematic component approaches the performance of the concatenated representation with half the latent dimensions, while latent interventions and component ablations support its role in generation. Qualitative results further demonstrate zero-shot human-torobot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Open-loop policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose SkeLAM, skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation. We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation. Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions. Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations. We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Action-conditioned robot world models. Robot world models support interactive simulation (Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a) and policy evaluation (Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026; Liao et al., 2025). Visual prediction supports foresight-guided policy learning (Lv et al., 2025a; Cai et al., 2026a) and multi-view data augmentation (Wang et al., 2026). Related research addresses video procedure planning (Ye et al., 2026), temporal answer grounding (Zhang et al., 2026), and cloudedge agent execution (Huang et al., 2026). DALI-R (Luo et al., 2026) reranks actions with 3D point-cloud latent predictions and task-completion scores. Control representations include action embeddings, skeleton sequences (Wang et al., 2025b; Wu & Gao, 2026), and kinematic renderings (Xu et al., 2026). Recent models further incorporate spatial grounding (Gu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). Separating camera and object motion also supports camera-controlled video generation (Cheng et al., 2026b). Latent action learning from videos. Latent action models encode visual transitions for world modeling (Bruce et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; 2026; Garrido et al., 2026) and robot policy learning (Ye et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Reconstruction-based learning is sensitive to distracting dynamics and ambiguous action correspondence (Nikulin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Olaf-World (Jiang et al., 2026) aligns integrated latent actions with temporal differences in frozen video features across contexts. LAOF (Bu et al., 2026b) uses agent optical flow as motion supervision to reduce sensitivity to distractors. Shared RGBdepth features provide geometric supervision (Govind et al., 2026), alongside advances in latent representations for policy learning (Liu et al., 2026a; Shen et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). LARYBench (Nie et al., 2026) evaluates representations using semantic action classification and physical action regression, independently of downstream policies. systematic study finds that proxy metrics support coarse model 2 Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models Figure 1: Overview of SkeLAM. SkeLAM grounds its kinematic component in robot skeletons while retaining complementary visual dynamics in separate residual. Structured action representations. Quantized skills support autoregressive action generation (Li et al., 2025), while flow-matching policies preserve latent-action structure and align latent and physical actions through interpolation-based sampling during decoder training (Lyu et al., 2026). Spatial and kinematic priors include voxel heatmaps (Yang et al., 2026c), robot graphs with differentiable kinematics (Lv et al., 2025b), and trajectories defined by endpoint positions and velocities (Lv et al., 2026). Joint image, LiDAR, and action modeling supports autonomous-driving trajectory generation (Cheng et al., 2026a). SkeleWAM (Sheng et al., 2026) jointly learns action and future-state prediction over sparse 3D robotobject skeletons. Skel-WAM (Cai et al., 2026b) cotrains visual and hand-skeleton dynamics on human and robot videos, with robot-trained action expert. SkeLAM uses skeleton supervision to ground video-derived kinematic latents for action-conditioned video prediction.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT
sections.content: We evaluate the effect of the kinematicresidual decomposition on action-conditioned world modeling, and examine motion transfer and rollout evaluation as downstream applications. Specifically, we investigate the following questions: RQ1 (World modeling): Does adapting robot actions to dedicated kinematic component improve motion accuracy while preserving visual fidelity? (Section 4.2) RQ2 (Motion representation): Do skeleton-grounded kinematic latents support more accurate linear decoding of robot motion than unstructured latent actions? (Section 4.3) RQ3 (Motion transfer): Can kinematic representation learned from robot interactions transfer human motion to generated robot rollouts in zero-shot setting? (Section 4.4) RQ4 (Policy evaluation): How closely do open-loop world-model rollouts reproduce policy rankings and success rates measured in real robot executions? (Section 4.5) 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Data. DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) pairs visual observations with robot actions, allowing us to assess whether predicted dynamics follow robot controls. We train the latent action model and world model on DROID, incorporating AgiBot (Bu et al., 2025) to broaden the range of robot interactions observed during training. Evaluation uses 400 DROID clips, each containing one conditioning frame and 12 future frames at 480 640 resolution. More details are provided in Appendix A. Evaluation Metrics. To quantify trajectory, direction, and magnitude agreement, we report 2D end-effector average displacement error (ADE, px), direction macro-F1 (F1dir), normalized magnitude MAE (Lmag ), and magnitude Pearson correlation (rmag). PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) assess pixel, structural, and perceptual fidelity, respectively, with tLPIPS reported as temporal diagnostic. More details are provided in Appendix C.1. 1 Implementation Details. We implement the latent action model using Transformer VAEs with dkin = dres = 32 and use Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B as the world-model backbone. We train with AdamW, using stage-specific learning rates and global batch sizes. SkeLAM training uses NVIDIA A100 GPUs and requires approximately 2 days for one complete run. Architectural specifications, loss weights, training schedules, and inference settings are provided in Appendix B. Baselines. We compare SkeLAM with latent-action world models DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) and CD-LAM (Wei et al., 2026). Alternative conditioning strategies include direct robot actions in IRASim (Zhu et al., 2025), Ctrl-World (Guo et al., 2026), Cosmos-Predict2.5 (Ali et al., 2025), Cosmos3 (Agarwal et al., 2026), and GE-Sim (Liao et al., 2025), and geometric guidance in EnerVerseAC (Jiang et al., 2025) and OSCAR (Wu & Gao, 2026). TesserAct (Zhen et al., 2025), and GEBase (Liao et al., 2025) serve as text-conditioned references for visual fidelity, with evaluation details provided in Appendix C. 4.2 ACTION-CONDITIONED WORLD MODELING Quantitative results. To assess how accurately SkeLAM simulates the consequences of robot actions, we evaluate motion accuracy and visual fidelity on DROID. Table 1 shows that SkeLAM ranks first on seven of eight metrics among the reported action-conditioned models, including all four visual fidelity metrics. Compared with DreamDojo and CD-LAM, SkeLAM reduces ADE by 19.5% and 23.7%, respectively, alongside LPIPS reductions of 11.1% and 17.4%. Ctrl-World and OSCAR achieve higher direction F1, while SkeLAM attains lower trajectory error and stronger visual fidelity. To examine how robot motion is encoded, we train linear probes on frozen latent representations. As shown in Table 3, the kinematic component achieves an EEF MAE of 5.99103 and magnitude macro-F1 of 0.7467, improving on both latent-action baselines. Within SkeLAM, it also outperforms the residual component on all three metrics. Concatenating the residual increases EEF R2 from 0.3200 to 0.3277 and magnitude macro-F1 from 0.7467 to 0.7482. The kinematic component thus approaches the probing performance of the full representation using half the latent dimensions, supporting its specialization for displacement and magnitude encoding. Cross-modal compatibility. To assess cross-modal motion conditioning, we intervene on the latent inputs to the RGB decoder. Figure 4 shows that substituting paired and mismatched skeleton kinematic means increases reconstruction MAE by 0.53% and 11.67%, respectively. SSIM exhibits the same ordering. Zeroing the kinematic component increases MAE by 5.78%, compared with 0.61% for the residual. The greater degradation under mismatched substitution than kinematic removal indicates sensitivity to motion correspondence. These results support compatible RGB and skeleton conditioning and functional role for the kinematic component in reconstruction. 4.4 ZERO-SHOT HUMAN-TO-ROBOT MOTION TRANSFER To examine whether the learned motion representation transfers across embodiments, we use human demonstration videos from UniSkill (Kim et al., 2025) as motion prompts. The RGB encoder extracts latent actions from these videos to directly condition SkeLAM, with robot observation specifying the initial scene. All model parameters remain fixed during transfer. We compare with the pretrained checkpoint of DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026), which supports latent-action conditioning. As shown in Figure 5, SkeLAM generates distinct end-effector motions corresponding to the human demonstrations: downward reach for the towel-pushing prompt and an upward movement for the tissue-pulling prompt. DreamDojo exhibits limited end-effector displacement in both examples. At the policy level, success-rate MAE decreases from 7.62 to 4.76 percentage points, with positive Spearman (ρ=0.5347) and Pearson (r=0.6091) correlations for SkeLAM. Together, these metrics indicate improved agreement in both absolute policy success rates and relative policy ordering. Figure 6 compares predicted and real success rates for individual policies, with proximity to the diagonal indicating closer agreement. The results support agreement in both individual task outcomes and relative policy performance under open-loop action replay. Nevertheless, the modest success recall indicates that reproducing successful task outcomes remains challenging. Further evaluation details are provided in Appendix C.3. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented SkeLAM, skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. The kinematic component provides motion-grounded target for robot action adaptation, while the residual retains complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction and branch dropout support reuse of the learned kinematic pathway for action-conditioned generation. Experiments on DROID show improved motion accuracy and visual fidelity, with representation analyses supporting kinematic specialization. Qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer, while policy evaluation yields success-rate estimates consistent with real robot executions. These results support structuring latent actions around robot motion while retaining complementary information for generation. Future work will extend the current recorded-action replay protocol to closed-loop policy evaluation. key question is how prediction errors affect subsequent policy decisions and task outcomes over longer interaction horizons.

sections.title: A DATA AND PREPROCESSING
sections.content: Data and splits. DROID and AgiBot World (Bu et al., 2025) are used in latent-action learning, world-model training, and action adaptation. DROID contributes 60,000 training clips to Stage 1 and 45,358 clips to each of Stages 2A, 2B, 3A, and 3B. RGB and skeleton observations are matched by episode, camera, and frame index; overlapping windows from an episode remain in the same partition. Normalization statistics are fitted on training data only. The DROID evaluation selects one clip from each of 400 trajectories: 100 trajectories per motion quartile, with additional camera stratification. AgiBot evaluation uses 400 held-out clips and 800 arm trajectories. Preprocessing. RGB and pre-rendered skeleton observations come from the corresponding OSCAR (Wu & Gao, 2026) subsets, following its kinematics, projection, and rasterization protocol. Stage 1 letterboxes both modalities to 240320 (height width): resize by min(240/Ho, 320/Wo) using OpenCV INTER AREA, round the resized dimensions, and center on zero canvas, assigning odd padding pixels to the bottom or right. Intensities are divided by 255. The target skeleton mask selects pixels with an 8-bit RGB channel sum above 15, then applies one dilation with 5 5 elliptical kernel. It is used only in the skeleton loss. Stage 2/3 uses 4:3 center crop resized to 480 640 for video generation; the frozen latent encoder keeps the Stage 1 resolution and uses the same source frame indices. Temporal alignment and action interface. DROID window samples 13 frames from 60-FPS video at indices fk = f0 + 4k, = 0, . . . , 12, giving 15 FPS and 0.8-second span; consecutive window starts differ by 24 source frames. The first frame conditions 12 future frames. Each transition pairs (ok, ok+1) with an executed state-delta proxy ak = [pk+1 pk; ωk; gk+1] R7, where translation is in the robot base frame, ωk is the rotation vector of the relative SO(3) rotation, and gk+1 is destination gripper openness. Deltas are between consecutive sampled states, not relative to the clip start or joint-space commands. Manifests retain source indices, timestamps, and transition-validity indicators. Deterministic latent extraction. The frozen Stage 1 RGB encoder exports posterior means as two 12 32 arrays, zkin and zres; the skeleton encoder is not used for world-model conditioning. Each component is standardized elementwise as = (z mz) max(sz, ϵ) using training statistics. The same kinematic statistics define adapter targets and world-model inputs; normalization is implicit in the main-text notation. Offline caches retain episode, camera, frame, preprocessing, and checkpoint identifiers and receive no gradients.
